prize_parts.citation: for establishing the empirical study of how legal institutions and investor protection shape financial development and corporate ownership

statement.case_for: Law and finance opened a new empirical field. It linked legal rules, investor protection, ownership concentration and the depth of financial markets in a cross-country framework. Corporate finance, comparative law and development research all adopted it, and it moved the question of why financial systems differ from description to testable hypotheses. As someone who works on financial contracting, I think its strongest lasting contribution is the set of facts and the research design, not the causal legal-origins story. The core papers are 25 or more years old, so replication, critique and refinement are well advanced. I would not make this prize turn on the strongest causal claims. The case is that the field exists because of this work and that it has been tested heavily enough to judge.
statement.case_against: The legal-origins thesis has been seriously challenged. Critics question the coding of legal rules and the anti-director index, whether legal origin is exogenous or proxies for history and other institutions, and how robust the results are. Excluding Vishny under the three-name cap is a real attribution cost, because he co-authored the founding papers. There is also a risk that the Committee would be rewarding a research programme whose headline mechanism has been qualified, and that the 2024 institutions prize makes the theme look less fresh.

responses.point: She ranks B001 only seventh. She sees the evidence as weaker than the influence, with concerns about how the legal-origins and anti-director indices were measured and coded, and about Shleifer's wide influence blurring attribution to this theme.
responses.response: I agree the measurement and causal-identification critiques are serious, and I have not tried to dismiss them. My view is that they qualify the mechanism more than they undermine the discovery. The cross-country regularities in ownership structure, market depth and investor protection, and the research agenda built on them, would survive even if the legal-origin story is only partly causal. On attribution, I would credit the specific legal-origins and investor-protection papers rather than Shleifer's whole record, and the citation is worded to do that. Where I differ from you is how much weight the critiques deserve relative to the field-creating contribution. I do not think they move this below the other candidates.

responses.point: She ranks B001 first for combining new cross-country data with an explanatory structure. She also flags that the causal case is less clean than the committee's recent preferences and that the three-name cap forces Vishny out, which is a binding attribution cost.
responses.response: I agree on both points. I would add that the cap forces a choice here that is not artificial. La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes and Shleifer carried the legal-origins and investor-protection programme across its many follow-ups, and Vishny's other main work lies in other areas. That makes the trio defensible, though not costless. On the identification concern, I would rest the citation on the research design and the established empirical facts, not on strong causal claims. That keeps us consistent with the standard we apply elsewhere.

responses.point: He ranks B001 fifth. He stresses methodological critiques, including measurement of legal rules, endogeneity of legal origin and replication concerns. He also notes that reputational and conduct controversies around individual authors could affect committee views, and that it is unresolved whether the mechanism is law or broader institutions and history.
responses.response: I take the methodological point seriously and agree that the law-versus-history question is open. I would answer that a prize can recognise the founding of a field even where its first causal story is only partly right. I cannot assess conduct controversies from the evidence supplied, and I do not think they should substitute for scientific evaluation here, so I treat them as an unresolved matter, not as part of the merit case. If the Committee wants a cleaner identification record, I would then look at B049 or B048 as alternatives, not at B001's rank.

responses.point: He ranks B015 first, citing the task framework, the race between education and technology, and the credible China-shock designs. He is candid that the three-name limit forces a choice between strands and that recent labour prizes may reduce room.
responses.response: I rank B015 fourth and agree on its quality and policy relevance. My hesitation is the attribution problem you describe, and that the task-framework theory overlaps with work already recognised in 2023 and 2024 and with the 2025 prize theme. A prize that credits only three names would leave out Dorn and others. I also see more risk of splitting a settled discovery across strands than for B001. If the Committee gives B015 more weight than I do, I would not oppose it, but I would want a citation that is clear about which strand is being honoured.

uncertainties: Whether the legal-origins hypothesis is judged to be a discovery in its own right, or whether the Committee will mainly credit the cross-country research design and facts.
How heavily to weigh the measurement and coding critiques of the investor-protection indices against the paradigm's reach across fields.
Whether the three-name cap, which excludes Vishny, would be seen as an unacceptable attribution cost.
Whether the 2024 institutions prize reduces the Committee's appetite for another award on institutions and finance.
Whether reputational concerns raised by colleagues, which are not documented in the supplied evidence, would bear on the Committee's judgement.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any credited candidate is documented in my supplied profile. My co-authors listed there (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner, Sørensen and others) are not on B001. I am an adjunct at Chicago Booth and work in corporate finance, which is close to this literature. I disclose that, without treating it as grounds for recusal. I have not independently verified any other affiliations of the credited names.
